Stock factors PSX investors often watch

Serious investors rarely buy on price charts alone. They gather evidence about the business, the balance sheet and the price they are asked to pay. This checklist is a starting map, not a scoring product and not a buy list.

Business quality and durability

Ask what the company sells, who pays, and why customers might stay. Read annual reports and result presentations instead of relying on a single tip.

A clear business model is easier to hold through volatility than a story you do not understand.

Growth, margins and returns

Look at whether revenue and profits are rising for believable reasons, and whether margins are stable or fragile.

Return measures such as return on equity can help, but only beside leverage and earnings quality — high ROE financed by dangerous debt is not free excellence.

Balance sheet and cash flow

Debt service, interest coverage and cash generation show how a company survives slowdowns. Paper profits with weak cash flow deserve extra scepticism.

Sector context matters: banks, manufacturers and funds do not share one “perfect” balance-sheet shape.

Valuation needs a peer frame

Multiples such as P/E only mean something next to growth, risk and comparable companies. Cheap can mean bargain or value trap.

Write down your assumptions before you anchor on a single ratio.

From research to personal records

After you buy, your outcome depends on your cost, fees, dividends and sell price. Tools like PSX Tracker keep that personal history straight while you continue learning how to analyse businesses.

A factor is a question, not a score

People say “quality” and “value” as if they were buttons. Each one is a pile of questions. Quality might mean the business earns high returns on the capital it uses, converts those earnings into cash, and does not depend on a single customer or a single raw material. Value might mean the price you pay is modest against those earnings, against the assets, or against the dividends. Neither question is answered by one ratio on one year.

A screen that sorts the whole market by one number will hand you a list of accounting accidents. A one-off gain, a change in depreciation, or a year of unusually low tax can make a company look cheap or profitable. Read the note under the number before you read the number.

This guide walks through the questions Pakistani investors commonly ask. It does not produce a ranking, and the app’s research pages are not a buy list when they show the same figures.

The business and its revenue

Start with what is sold, to whom, and what it costs to deliver. A cement plant, a bank, and a software exporter do not share a useful “average margin.” Compare a company with its own history and with peers that do the same thing. The cement and bank guides on this site are examples of that peer reading.

Concentration is a factor even when it is not in a screener. One product, one buyer, one concession, or one regulated price means the future is a single decision someone else makes. You can still own it. You should know you own that decision.

Growth is only pleasant when the company can fund it. Growth funded by endless new shares or by debt that the cash flow cannot service is a different factor, leverage, wearing a cheerful name.

Profit, cash, and the gap between them

Profit is an opinion the accounts assemble under a standard. Cash from operations is closer to the bank. A company that reports rising profit and weak operating cash, year after year, is asking you to believe in receivables, capitalization policies, or both. Read the cash-flow statement, not only the earnings line the ratio used.

Margins tell you what is left after the direct costs. They move when input prices move. For a manufacturer, energy and raw materials can dominate. For a bank, the interesting “margin” is the net interest margin, which is a different construction entirely. Do not drop both into one column and sort.

One excellent year is a story. Five ordinary years are a pattern. Factors that depend on a single year will rank the lucky and the aggressive above the steady. Look at the run of years in the financials panel or, better, in the annual reports.

Leverage and dilution

Debt matters because the lender gets paid before you do. The useful questions are how much, at what cost, secured against what, and what happens if the main profit source dips. A low debt number in a business that does not need debt is different from a low debt number in a business that usually carries a lot and happens to be between projects.

New shares matter because your fraction of the business shrinks. A rising profit shared with a much larger number of shares can leave earnings per share flat. Read the share count. Bonus issues and splits change the count without new money. Rights issues change the count and ask you for money. Record which one happened so your per-share history stays honest.

Related-party loans and guarantees often sit in the notes, not in the headline ratio. If the company is lending to its sponsors or borrowing from them, that is part of the factor, not a footnote you skip.

Valuation is the price of the other factors

A fine business at a reckless price can be a poor investment. A mediocre business at a distressed price can be a fine one, or a trap. The P/E guide covers one common yardstick and the ways it misleads. Price to book, dividend yield, and enterprise measures against cash flow are other yardsticks. Use more than one, and use them against peers.

The price half of every valuation ratio is today’s market. It changes while you are reading. The earnings half changes when the next accounts arrive. A ratio without a date is not a fact you can file.

No combination of factors removes the chance of being wrong. The point of writing them down is to know why you bought and what would make you revisit. The tracker can hold the position and the notes. It cannot hold the conviction for you.

Common questions

What is a factor in this guide?

A measurable trait investors compare, such as profitability, debt, cash generation, or valuation. None of them is a buy signal by itself.

Should I rank stocks on one ratio?

No. A single ratio ignores the business, the balance sheet, and whether the accounts are comparable.

Does PSX Tracker recommend stocks from these factors?

No. Research screens are context for your own work.
